overview.headline: Deep time from early rock laws to modern radiometric dating

keyPoints.point: Earth has an ancient age spanning billions of years of deep time.
keyPoints.quote: Earth is 4.54 billion years old, a span of time that is hard for many people to grasp.

keyPoints.point: Basic stratigraphy principles allow observers to order geologic events as relative time without absolute age.
keyPoints.quote: allow observers to put geologic events in order to tell the story of relative time, but they don’t provide an absolute age.

keyPoints.point: Uniformitarianism states that processes happening on Earth today shaped Earth in the past.
keyPoints.quote: states that the processes that we see happening on Earth today are the same processes that shaped Earth in the past

keyPoints.point: Faunal succession states that characteristic fossils of a certain age mark that age everywhere.
keyPoints.quote: which states that species become extinct and are replaced by new species, and that characteristic fossils of a certain age are that age everywhere.

keyPoints.point: Patterson used lead-lead dating to determine the age of Canyon Diablo meteorite.
keyPoints.quote: used lead-lead dating to determine that the Canyon Diablo meteorite was 4.55 billion years old.

keyTerms.gloss: concept of vast geologic history over long spans
keyTerms.quote: is the concept of deep time.

keyTerms.gloss: law that older rocks lie below younger rocks
keyTerms.quote: The law of superposition says that older rocks are on the bottom and younger rocks are on the top.

keyTerms.gloss: principle that present processes shaped past geology
keyTerms.quote: proposed what would become the foundational principle of geology — uniformitarianism.

keyTerms.quote: In 1815, Smith developed the law of faunal succession, which states that species become extinct
